Beyond the training itself, I gained confidence in my ability to grow through adversity and a deeper appreciation for the selfless service of those who serve our country. Special thanks to MIs Brendan Turner, Colin Crecelius, Ollie White, Ciara Carter, and William Reed for your mentorship and investment in our development. The camaraderie within our company made the experience unforgettable. I'm excited to begin the next chapter this fall as a Naval ROTC Midshipman at the University of Pennsylvania. We just made a customer's robots 30% faster AND 7% more successful. We never touched their hardware. Two most important KPIs for these robots in prod: faster and fewer failures. We used RL to improve both, which was not possible for them prior to working with us. This is because RL needs thousands of rollouts and feedback on which behaviors are better, and on a physical robot that means days of ops time. So we did all of it inside our world model simulator. Their policy runs closed-loop in our sim exactly as it does on hardware, which means we can roll out and evaluate candidate behaviors at massive scale, in parallel, with zero robot time. Inside that sim, we trained a small RL model that makes their policy faster and more reliable: trimming the wasted motion and editing out the failure modes. To prove this actually worked, they deployed our RL model on their real robots and evaluated the two head to head (base policy vs. base + RL): interleaved A/B on matched scenes, 2,000 episodes over a week, every episode human-rated. With our RL model on top, the robots delivered 30% more successful completions per robot-hour (p < 0.001), and task success rate improved 7% in absolute terms (p = 0.0008)! The improvement we measured in sim is the improvement they measured on hardware. No sim-to-real gap. Now the flywheel is running: their fleet collects scenes in production, every scene rolls out in our world model, new failures and slow behavior surface in sim, and an improved RL model ships on top of their unchanged policy. Each turn of the loop, the robots get faster and more reliable. No need to spend weeks wrangling with robot operators and hardware inconsistencies or waiting months for a new foundation model. publications.title: Improving Height Estimation for Stationary Targets with 3D Automotive Radar: From Uncertainty Analysis to Temporal Filtering
publications.subtitle: IEEE Transactions on Radar Systems
publications.description: This paper addresses the challenge of elevation angle estimation in 3D automotive radar, a critical limitation for achieving accurate and reliable 3D scene understanding in autonomous driving. While vertical Doppler Beam Sharpening (DBS) provides a foundation for height estimation, existing implementations often suffer from limitations due to measurement noise. We enhance DBS using a rigorous uncertainty analysis and a robust, temporal filtering approach. Our analysis reveals the significant impact of target-sensor geometry, particularly small elevation angles, on estimation errors. To mitigate these uncertainties, we develop a simple yet effective method combining an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for temporal filtering with robust data association to reject spurious detections. Real-world experiments on highway and ITRI campus datasets, spanning 34 km and 1.9 km respectively, using a standard 3D radar and a pre-built LiDAR map for ground truth, demonstrate a substantial improvement in height accuracy. Compared to unfiltered DBS, our method increases height accuracy within 1 meter from 53.41% to 62.32% on the highway and from 47.74% to 57.56% on ITRI campus.

publications.title: Automotive Radar Missing Dimension Reconstruction from Motion
publications.subtitle: 2023 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
publications.description: Automotive radars have been reliably used in most assisted and autonomous driving systems due to their robustness to extreme weather conditions. With radial velocity measurements from automotive radars, moving targets such as cars, trucks, and buses can be tracked robustly. However, due to the lack of elevation angles in measurements from automotive radars, stationary targets at different heights, such as maintenance holes and bridges, cannot be distinguished. Most autonomous systems rely on sensor fusion or ignore stationary targets to tackle the problem of missing the elevation angle dimension, which derives safety issues. We propose a simple yet effective approach to estimate the elevation angles of stationary targets from relative velocity and radial velocity measurements from an automotive radar. In contrast to structure from motion in computer vision, we utilize the instantaneous velocity generated from the motion of the ego vehicle. The radial velocity of each target is the projection of relative velocity onto the radial direction from radar to target. The radial velocity of each target can be inferred given the target's azimuth, elevation angle, and relative velocity. Accordingly, the elevation angle of each stationary target can be uniquely calculated given the velocity of radar and the target's azimuth and radial velocity measurements. The radar's velocity is estimated with the existing radar odometry algorithm and IMU. The proposed method is verified with real-world data. We evaluate the system's performance with a pre-built point cloud map and a good localization module in a real-world scenario. The proposed elevation angle reconstruction can reach a 1.41-degree mean error and standard deviation of 0.6 degrees in elevation angle.

publications.title: Extrinsic and Temporal Calibration of Automotive Radar and 3D LiDAR in Factor and On-Road Calibration Settings
publications.subtitle: IEEE Open Journal of Intelligent Transportation Systems
publications.description: While automotive radars are widely used in ADAS and autonomous driving, extrinsic and temporal calibration of automotive radars with other sensors is still daunting due to the sparsity, uncertainty, and missing elevation angles of automotive radar measurements. We propose a target-based calibration approach of 3D automotive radar and 3D LiDAR that performs extrinsic and temporal calibration in both factory and on-road settings. In factory calibration settings, a map is built with precise target poses; target trajectories are estimated based on map-based target localization in which the accuracy of both nearby and faraway target pose estimates can be ensured. The spatial and temporal relationships between radar and LiDAR measurements are established with target trajectories to accomplish extrinsic and temporal calibration. The proposed data collection procedure provides sufficient motion for analyzing time delay between sensors and can significantly reduce the data collection effort and time. There is 52.3% distance error reduction after time delay compensation in the experiment, which shows the improvements of temporal calibration. In on-road calibration settings, the metal objects with semantic labels, such as traffic signs, are selected as calibration targets. Although there could be insufficient correspondences to infer the missing dimension of planar radar for six DoF extrinsic calibration as demonstrated in factory calibration settings, the three extrinsic parameters and the time delay are shown still to be accurate. We validated the proposed method using the nuScenes datasets, which provide sensor measurements, poses, and HD map. With twenty-two data logs, each has over 1000 correspondences, the result of extrinsic parameters reaches centimeter-level accuracy compared with the offered benchmark. The time delay compensation improves 1 meter error for radar tracking in a 20 m/s vehicle case and improves mapping quality in real world data.

projects.title: Boosting Stochastic Trajectory Prediction using Conditional Latent Diffusion Model
projects.description: Initiated and co-led development of a stochastic trajectory prediction system using a conditional latent diffusion model; proposed semantic traffic fusion, significantly boosting accuracy:Trajectory prediction is a trending topic recent years. There are various deep learning models designed to do predict the trajectories of vehicles and pedestrians in driving scenes. Most of the competitions require models to predict multiple predictions and focus on evaluating the nearest prediction to the ground truth. A typical way to perform trajectory prediction is using Transformer model to fuse the information of vehicles' history trajectories, lane lines, and other information. However, we think of this task as a generative task, and should be solved in a different manner. Those Transformer based model can perform well on statistics overall, but cannot really hold a good variety of generated predictions. If think of the task of generative task, Transformer based models are kind of auto-regressive approach, which has been replaced with VAE, GAN, or Diffusion models in image generation recent years. We propose a Diffusion based trajectory prediction model that can generate predictions with good variety.

We stress-tested some AI detectors and found that they rarely flag human text as AI-generated. But asking LLMs to mimic a specific author causes detectors to misclassify text as human-generated ~13% of the time. For scientific writing, false negatives rose to ~26%. We asked Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro to generate 500-word passages mimicking 99 different authors across blogging, fiction, and scientific writing. We gave the models 5 samples of each author’s work as reference. False negatives were concentrated in scientific writing. GPTZero missed 24% of author-mimicking scientific passages, Pangram missed 25%, and Originality missed 29%. We also tested the detectors on legitimate human text, and on AI text generated from basic prompts with no examples or mimicry instructions. Detectors were reliable on both, with most avoiding more than a 1% error rate in either category. Read the full Data Insight and methodology: https://lnkd.in/e27QADVg ...more ...more

What are the largest software engineering tasks AI can perform? To answer this, we built MirrorCode, our long-horizon SWE benchmark that lets AI code autonomously for days at a time. The best models complete some tasks we estimate would take human engineers several weeks. In MirrorCode, AI models are given execute-only access to a program, docs, and tests demonstrating intended behavior. The AI must then reimplement the program from scratch. The model’s output is graded against a suite of tests, including held-out tests to prevent cheating. MirrorCode features 25 target programs spanning different areas of computing: Unix utilities, data serialization and query tools, bioinformatics, interpreters, static analysis, cryptography, and compression. AI can solve many long-horizon MirrorCode tasks. E.g., Claude Opus 4.7 passed 99.95% of tests when reimplementing gotree — a bioinformatics toolkit with 16k lines of Go and 40+ commands. We estimate this would take an engineer 2–17 weeks. Opus 4.7 solved it in 14 hours for $251. MirrorCode is not fully solved. The best headline score so far is 56% from Opus 4.7, meaning there is significant room for improvement. When models fall short, they often make substantial progress — passing 90% or more of tests — but fail on edge cases. MirrorCode has three advantages over many SWE benchmarks: 1. It’s difficult but practically solvable. 2. It scales up inference to better measure the limits of AI performance. 3. It’s resistant to cheating. MirrorCode tasks are difficult, but solvable. Unlike recent reverse-engineering benchmarks, MirrorCode is about implementing software to satisfy a detailed spec. AIs could realistically score 100% without needing to guess which (possibly undocumented) features they should cover. MirrorCode scales up inference spending to better measure AI’s limits. Many SWE benchmarks cap inference around $1–10 per task, even when the work would take weeks for a skilled human. One of the longest MirrorCode runs lasted 19 days and cost $2,600. MirrorCode resists cheating by design. We sandbox AIs: no internet access, no way to get the original source code, no hacking the scorer. Models never see held-out tests while developing their code, so they cannot cheat by creating a lookup table against the original program. MirrorCode lets us study other aspects of AI SWE performance. Can AIs code equally well in different programming languages? On MirrorCode tasks, there’s little sign of programming language affecting AI performance, even in obscure languages like Ada. We are releasing 22 of 25 MirrorCode programs as open source to support future research on long-horizon SWE capabilities. We are keeping three programs as a held-out set. Find the MirrorCode leaderboard and full paper analyzing results on our website: epoch.ai/MirrorCode MirrorCode was co-developed with METR and supported by a METR grant. ...more ...more

Congrats to Jim Ventre , Phillips Academy 's 17th head of school (seated in Sheldon's spot with John Palfrey, who was the 15th). Jim taught my first English class at Andover, maybe in his first year as a teaching fellow, in an ambitiously titled course called Competence. It met at 8:00 a.m., and for one of our first classes Jim got a big blue Suburban from the school and drove us down the hill to McDonald's. He bought us hash browns and told us to spend the rest of class writing about what we saw. I was thrilled. At my old public high school, there was a McDonald's across the street, and kids got in trouble for going there during the school day. Rather than trying to tell us about the importance of observation in your writing, he showed us. I'm still grateful to Jim for his efforts to make me a more competent writer, and to all the other amazing teachers I still remember fondly, including Gregory Wilkin , who passed around a cold can of beans for us to eat while talking about Hemingway; Victor Svec, who climbed out a third-floor window and back in again, then did a Superfly onto his desk to teach us the Russian words for "in" and "on"; John Strudwick and his riveting economic history of the United States; and every Craig Thorn class ever. Andover's students today are as lucky as I was back in that McDonald's.

publications.title: Proximal State Nudging: Reducing Skill Atrophy from AI Assistance
publications.subtitle: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026
publications.description: Presented in person in Seoul, South KoreaSkill atrophy, the gradual decline of human capability under AI assistance, poses a safety risk in shared-control of semi-autonomous systems, where operators may be unable to distinguish their own inputs from autonomous corrections. We propose Proximal State Nudging (PSN), a shared autonomy algorithm that jointly optimizes for skill development and task performance by nudging users toward states estimated to be most learnable. We first show that PSN outperforms existing shared autonomy baselines in balancing student improvement in unassisted reward with overall shared performance, using simulated students in the classic LunarLander environment. We then present, to the best of our knowledge, the first human subject studies of a planner incorporating learning-compatible shared autonomy: across two driving tasks in the CARLA simulator (High Performance Racing and Parallel Parking, n = 60), PSN produces up to 7x larger gains in unassisted skill than standard blended shared autonomy, while incurring 50 fewer collisions than unassisted self-practice.

publications.title: Intent at a Glance: Gaze-Guided Robotic Manipulation via Foundation Models
publications.subtitle: Robotics: Science & Systems (RSS) 2025
publications.description: Presented in person in Los Angeles, CaliforniaDesigning intuitive interfaces for robotic control remains a central challenge in enabling effective human-robot interaction, particularly in assistive care settings. Eye gaze offers a fast, non-intrusive, and intent-rich input modality, making it an attractive channel for conveying user goals. In this work, we present GAMMA (Gaze Assisted Manipulation for Modular Autonomy), a system that leverages ego-centric gaze tracking and a vision-language model to infer user intent and autonomously execute robotic manipulation tasks. By contextualizing gaze fixations within the scene, the system maps visual attention to high-level semantic understanding, enabling skill selection and parameterization without task-specific training. We evaluate GAMMA on a range of table-top manipulation tasks and compare it against baseline gaze-based control without reasoning. Results demonstrate that GAMMA provides robust, intuitive, and generalizable control, highlighting the potential of combining foundation models and gaze for natural and scalable robot autonomy. publications.description: Presented in person at Santa Fe, New MexicoSwim pose estimation and recognition is a challenging problem in machine learning and artificial intelligence as the body of the swimmer is continuously submerged under the water. publications.title: Design and Analysis of an FPGA-based CNN for Exercise Recognition
publications.subtitle: IEEE TRON Symposium (TRONSHOW 2023)
publications.description: Presented by first author Derrick Trinh (virtually) in TRON Symposium, hosted in Tokyo, JapanIn this paper, we describe the design and analysis of an FPGA-based exercise detector, and show the improvement in performance of an FPGA-based over a GPU-based human action recognition application. Using the Xilinx Kria KV260 development board and a USB webcam, the pose of a person is tracked to determine what kind of exercise they are doing. OpenPose is used to obtain the coordinates of a person’s body parts. Using Vitis AI and Tensorflow, multiple neural networks to identify different exercises were designed using a sequence of the coordinates as an input. These models have different input sizes and number of convolutional layers. These neural network models were run directly on the programmable logic (Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA) of the Kria board, and their performance in frames per second (FPS) was analyzed. Our simulation results show that the FPGA’s performance based on a relatively simple CNN reached 372 to 722 FPS while the ResNet-based GPU (Jetson Nano) performance was 32 FPS, for which the accuracy degradation is less than 10%.

activity.title: I'm at #ICML2026 🇰🇷 to present our new work on reducing skill atrophy from AI overreliance with Toyota Research Institute ! As AI systems improve their capabilities, how can we use them to also support a human user’s own skill development? At the #AI4GOOD workshop, I’ll be presenting Proximal State Nudging (PSN): an assistance algorithm that balances between task performance and human learning. https://lnkd.in/gShT9nUn We were inspired by control tasks (surgery, driving, teleoperation) where AI has been shown to improve task safety and performance, but also has a deskilling effect on people! For example: • Medicine ( https://lnkd.in/gynVuqqx ) • Driving ( https://lnkd.in/g5ddkbpa ) • Coding ( https://lnkd.in/g-pcKaVw ) Prior works often remove AI support entirely so that people can learn. PSN offers a new option: modulate *how* AI assistance is given in order to both ensure safe performance and scaffold human learning. PSN works by (i) estimating which environment states are most “learnable” for an individual user, and then (ii) adjusting the *level* and *type” of AI assistance to gradually nudge the user to these states, while still optimizing for task reward. Similar to how a parent might hold and help their kid learning how to ride a bike! 😊 We evaluate PSN in both the Lunar Lander environment and with 60 human participants in two CARLA driving tasks: parallel parking and high-performance racing. PSN produced up to 7x gains in unassisted skill learning compared to standard shared autonomy methods, while incurring 50% fewer collisions than unassisted self-practice. This is joint work with Yuchen Cui Deepak Gopinath, PhD Emily Sumner, PhD and Guy Rosman , and I’ll be at ICML if interested in learning more! ...more ...more

So....how are students expected to figure out which university recruiter is supposed to be recruiting for what? I highkey think it is running it down mid when people encourage students to reach out to recruiters, but not specify to them the person they're reaching out to might not (A) be a university recruiter in the first place, (B) be the aligned recruiter for what they're interested in, or (C) be someone that can even help. All the while, they burn their precious InMail credits in doing so. I think students are frustrated with recruiting because they don't know who is responsible for what, because they believe that knowing will give them an edge. At the same time, I am experienced enough to know that everyone has different worldviews when it comes to their social media and privacy, and a response is not owed. Which is why most recruiters might not be respond to LinkedIn messages. The thing is, if it stands that there are those who don't respond to messages, it stands to reason that some 𝐦𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭. In that vein, my reminder to my students is this - congratulation posts and announcement posts do serve a purpose, and this can help if you plan ahead. When written on LinkedIn , students usually thank their recruiting coordinators, sourcers, and/or university recruiters that they've worked with. I can happily confirm this because I'm tagged in these posts. So if that connection of yours has the internship/new grad role you're specifically interested in, they likely have survived the recruiting process and those people they've thanked, were 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐝 with their recruiting in that genre of internship. hint >_> hint >_> !!!! hint >_> !!!!!!!!!!!!! Check their profiles. Check their job title. Check their posts. Use context clues to come to a conclusion. Then, send a message respectfully. And be mindful of the calendar too! The world is a big place and recruiters are 𝐧𝐨𝐭 all the same. In the vein that some recruiters don't respond to everyone, then there has to be recruiters that sincerely try when they can. So it is my hope that this advice helps students find those rare recruiters, because I promise that they do exist! I choose to believe that there are recruiters out there that do fight the good fight and when they find windows for air, they respond where they can. Whether they are able to help depends entirely on circumstance, so please be mature enough to accept this. I do believe there are lots of kind recruiters out there, because I choose to believe there are kind people. Just this past Tuesday night, when I finished babysitting my Codex "/goal" and went to bed, I did not expect to wake up at 3AM to a message saying that my role at the Amazon AGI SF Lab had been eliminated. It turned out that it was not just me—the entire lab had been shut down. I am still processing the news, but I have calmed down enough to reflect on my one year and two months at the lab. It was my first full-time job, and it was a team and mission that I cared about deeply. Looking back, the feeling that stands out most is gratitude. First, I want to thank my manager, Xiangjun (XJ) Wang , for allowing me to enter the world of large-scale reinforcement learning for agent training. I still remember we started on veRL, added vision-language model(VLM) support, and integrated internal WebGym environments so we could train RL exceeding 1,000 steps, and we delivered Nova Act at last year’s re:Invent, pushing the frontier of computer-use agents(CUA). This year, with only two engineers, we migrated to Slime to take advantage of its modular architecture and stronger support for asynchronous RL. We improved its fully asynchronous training, added support for long-horizon agent training, and ultimately used it to train a 100B MoE model that achieved 70 on SWE-bench Verified and 45 on Terminal-Bench, surpassing GPT-OSS, Nemotron 3 super, and Gemm4 31B. After DeepSeek V4 was released, we decided to scale our RL even further, toward models with more than 1T+ parameters. We migrated to Miles for faster support of open-source models and better compatibility with Blackwell GPUs. We were almost there. The mid-train was nearly complete. The RL data was ready. And then, everything stopped. I am equally grateful to my talented and extraordinarily reliable colleagues. You have been my closest friends, collaborators, and teachers. One of the things I valued most about this team was that there was no rigid boundary between infra and algorithms. Cross-disciplinary collaboration was not only encouraged—it was essential. Many of the hardest problems in RL require expertise from both sides. For example, truncated importance sampling(TIS) is an algo solution to a difficult systems problem: the mismatch between training and inference engines. Our fully asynchronous RL training recipe was also the result of close collaboration between infrastructure and algorithm researchers. Also, as someone who wants to understand the entire stack, I learned far more than infra alone. PPO, GRPO, value functions, etc., are no longer black boxes to me; data triage and curation were equally fascinating; I learned which metrics matter for evaluating an RL run. The list goes on. This experience will remain one of the highlights of my life. I will remember this team, the problems we tackled, and everything we built together. I wish everyone the very best, and I sincerely hope our paths cross again. Finally, I am open to new opportunities. #OpenToWork

activity.title: Buildbox (YC S26) finds user-facing agent failures hidden behind successful traces and evals. The most expensive agent failures rarely look like errors. An agent can pass its evals and look healthy in traces while still failing to help users complete important tasks. They ask again, redirect the agent, try a workaround, or give up. Teams usually uncover these patterns after they’ve already affected customers. Buildbox is agent analytics built around user outcomes. We find where important journeys break down, show how often it happens and who it affects, and connect those failures to activation, conversion, and retention. Buildbox then tests better agent behaviors and product experiences, giving teams evidence-backed fixes to review and ship. Founders Mark Nour and Trishala Jain met at UC Berkeley and have been building together for the past three years. Across teams at Netflix, Google, Amazon, and MongoDB, they saw the same pattern: companies had plenty of signals & observability, but finding the issues that actually mattered and turning them into a fix still took a lot of manual detective work. Building something from 0 is hard, and you don’t see the thousands of people building for years before things take off. Don’t let someone else’s highlight reel make you feel behind. 𝟮. 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝘀𝗸. Want an introduction? Want to meet someone? Want to try something you don’t feel qualified for? Ask. People are much more willing to help than you’d expect. 𝟯. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗹𝗮𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘀. Social media makes building look like vibecoding an app in a week, landing huge contracts, and going viral. The reality is a lot of rejection, and questioning yourself every day. The highs are incredibly rewarding, but they come with some pretty low lows. 𝟰. 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗲𝗱 >>>> I’ve learned more from shipping and talking to users than I ever did from planning to start a company. The best way to learn is by "actually doing the thing". 𝟱. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿. Make time for people, coffee can turn into a friendship, a cold DM can turn into a customer, and a random introduction can completely change your trajectory. Building a company is a people game first. Moving to SF has introduced me to some of the smartest and most ambitious I’ve ever met (shout out Ethan Wang & Mann Bellani ) Still learning + building more & more every day.

I'm an incoming senior and here's 10 pieces of advice I'd give to my 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗻 self: 𝟭. 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 — 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝘀𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻. Join things. Try things. Research things. But you don't need to be in 5 clubs doing 5 different projects. Depth > breadth. 𝟮. 𝗝𝗼𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗯𝘀. Clubs are the best way to build community and meet people with similar career goals. Some of my closest friends came from orgs I joined freshman year. 𝟯. 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺𝘀. Freshman-specific programs exist for a reason. If you want my list of 700+ programs, send me a connection request with a note. 𝟰. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄. I did a journalism internship because I thought I wanted to go into journalism. I realized I didn't and pivoted. I wouldn't have known that unless I experienced it. 𝟱. 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀. Think about a double major or minor. Map out your GEs early so you're not scrambling senior year. 𝟲. 𝗦𝗮𝘆 𝘆𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂. That first networking event. That cold DM. That application you feel unqualified for. Do it anyway. 𝟳. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿. Someone 1-2 years ahead who can show you what's possible and what to avoid. They've been where you are — learn from them. 𝟴. 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗚𝗣𝗔 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸. But don't let it tank either. Balance academics with real-world experience. 𝟵. 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽. Professors, career centers, peers — most freshmen suffer in silence when resources are right there. Don't be afraid to reach out. 𝟭𝟬. 𝗘𝗻𝗷𝗼𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿. It's the most stress-free year you're going to have. Seriously. Soak it in. Freshman year sets the foundation for everything that comes after. I did everything from: - doing three clubs - applying to mentorship programs - adding a minor that I later decided not to do - landing an internship and a lot more random side quests that led me to figure out what I wanted to do. You don't need to have it all figured out — but you do need to start. We’re beyond excited to officially introduce Intelligence. We raised a $7.9M seed, led by Index Ventures with participation from Conviction , A*, and Y Combinator , to build Design Arena , a universal interface for accessing and evaluating the world’s AI capabilities. We built Design Arena because we noticed that models were bad at making things “look good,” so we built a product that was both for humans to use to access design intelligence and for models to use to understand what designs humans want. The idea is simple: People come to Design Arena with a request. Models compete to fulfill the request, and users determine what works best for them. We use that real-world feedback to evaluate models, improve how work is routed, and help people access the right intelligence. Despite its simplicity, the scale of this idea exceeded our wildest expectations: In 6 months, we scaled from $5M to $60M ARR and 5.5M users across 190+ countries as a team of 10, and there’s no slowing down. We’ve helped the world’s leading frontier labs break the news on their state-of-the-art model capabilities. And the best part about it? We play with the models for a living to find out their limits. What’s the limit? Well, you’ll have to join us to find out :)

Hey guys, might have made one of the fastest frontend frameworks till date over the past two weeks! Firstly, Next.js pages are just JavaScript that returns HTML. So why do you need 300MB of dependencies to serve one? That bugged me. After nanobrew (1.2MB replacing 57MB Homebrew) and mcp-zig (131KB replacing 52MB of TypeScript), I couldn't not try the obvious next thing. So I built merjs. A Next.js-style web framework written entirely in Zig. Zero node_modules. 2MB binary. Ships to Cloudflare Workers. https://merlionjs.com (it's a 5kB page) Here's what routing looks like: ``` app/index.zig / app/weather.zig /weather api/ai.zig /api/ai ``` Drop a .zig file. Export render(). Run one command. Route is live. No config files. No webpack. No "oh you need to install these 17 peer dependencies first." I also built Claude Code skills for it. View them here: https://lnkd.in/grCjyHjY So you can just type `/new-page dashboard` or `/new-api users` or `/deploy` and it scaffolds the whole thing for you. Pages, API routes, WASM modules, dev server, full deploy. You don't even need to know Zig to get started. Just tell Claude what you want. The demo is a real Singapore government data dashboard. Live weather, air quality, UV index, all pulled from data.gov.sg . Not a todo app. A real thing running on Cloudflare Workers right now. https://lnkd.in/gsGsdrKm The deeper bet here is that WebAssembly breaks the last reason Node.js owned the server. JS won because it ran in the browser. Now Zig can too. Write your server in Zig, compile client logic to .wasm, ship it. No bundler. No hydration. One language, two targets. 2MB binary. 2,400+ req/s. Zero node_modules. Built in Singapore. Still very experimental but it works. Someone found a faster algorithm than Dijkstra's after 69 years. And that's absolutely wild. Time to drop some graph theory lore. Dijkstra invented his single-source shortest-path algorithm in 1956, and it is remarkable for how long it has stood as the best deterministic algorithm for this problem. Since then, the only improvements have come from tweaking the priority queue, culminating with Fibonacci heaps in the 1980's, yielding a runtime of O(E + V log V) (if you want to review Dijkstra's algorithm, see https://lnkd.in/gGhsmuJJ ). And then, out of nowhere, a new 2025 paper, "Breaking the Sorting Barrier for Directed Single-Source Shortest Paths" (by Ran Duan, Jiayi Mao, Xiao Mao, Xinkai Shu, and Longhui Yin) comes out with a new O(E * (log V)^0.67)-time algorithm. This beats Dijkstra for sparse graphs. To see how crazy that is, compare it with the table below, which shows the slow, gradual improvements for another classic graph problem: the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) problem. Dijkstra's reign lasted so long that it was widely believed to be optimal. In fact, if I read between the lines, it seems that the legendary Robert E Tarjan (co-inventor of the Fibonacci heap mentioned above, and who is all over the MST table below) has recently been trying to prove that Dijkstra's algorithm is truly optimal. Two of his most recent papers, "Bidirectional Dijkstra's Algorithm is Instance-Optimal" (2024) and "Universal Optimality of Dijkstra via Beyond-Worst-Case Heaps" (2023), chip away at showing how Dijkstra is optimal in different aspects, almost--but not quite--precluding the new result! 1956-2025. What a run. ...more ...more

Just took 3rd place at the OpenAI × Start2 × Zendesk Hackathon at the Hanwha AI Center. How? Here's the explanation: Most AI support tools break the moment someone can't hand them a clean sentence. We spent a weekend building one that doesn't need the sentence at all. We call it Wordless. Two million Americans live with aphasia. They understand everything you say to them, they just can't always retrieve the words to say back what's wrong. Ask someone mid-anomia to describe a billing error and you might get a bunch of random words: "order… wrong… the thing… help." Every support agent on the market reads that, grabs the nearest-sounding help article, and closes the ticket confidently wrong. Wordless doesn't ask the person to explain. It figures it out. The moment a request comes in, it reads the customer's actual account - recent charges, orders, past tickets - and flags what's most likely broken. Two identical charges thirty seconds apart? That's the problem, and no one had to type the word "duplicate." Whatever fragment the person can offer gets matched by meaning, not spelling, so "the boily thing" still lands on their kettle order. Then it lays out the top few guesses as big tap-to-confirm cards. Four words in, one tap out. Under the hood: Composio for the account reads, Octen for the semantic matching, Codex generating the interface live, Zendesk closing the loop. We were the only high school team there, and it was our first hackathon - so hearing our name called for one of 5 selected presentation slots, then again for 3rd place, was not something we saw coming. Huge thanks to Nick Lum , founder of BeeLine Reader, who spent real time speaking to us about his experiences and sharpening how we thought about the whole thing. Grateful for that. And to my teammates Avinash Amanchi , Akshat Agarwal and Rushil Baindla - this was all of us. Thanks to OpenAI , Composio , Octen AI , Zendesk , and Start2 Group for hosting such a great event. More coming.
